newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong people come to grips with being Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong people come to grips with being Chinese.

text.p: The handover party is finally over, and Hong Kong is firmly nestled in the Chinese fold.
But the territory's former British subjects are just coming to grips with the reality that they are now part of communist China -- albeit a capitalist part.
"I thought I was prepared for the moment, but when I heard the Chinese national anthem at midnight, I was just stunned," said Wendy Cheung, a 22-year-old typist.
"I thought, oh my God, I'm now what? Part of this mass of 1.2, 1.3 billion people," she said.
Britain handed its former colony of 156 years back to China at midnight on June 30 in a grand ceremony attended by thousands of foreign dignitaries, VIPs and members of the world's media.
The event was beamed live via satellite to televisions around the globe.

Fluttering atop most major buildings in Hong Kong, now called a Special Administrative Region of China, is China's red national flag with its five golden stars, and Hong Kong's new flag, emblazoned with its tropical blossom emblem, the bauhinia.

Under Sino-British treaties on Hong Kong's handover, the territory is promised a high degree of autonomy for the next 50 years under a unique "one country, two systems" formula set by China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
It's business as usual, says new leader Tung Chee-hwa.

But an undercurrent of concern has built up since Tung gave new powers to police to ban protests in the name of "national security", froze labour rights laws, launched a plan to trim back democracy and prepared to deport child illegal immigrants.
A China-anointed provisional legislature, which replaced an elected chamber at the handover, is also expected to be assailed by a flurry of lawsuits challenging its legality in the coming weeks.
Some Hong Kong people, who live in one of the world's most prosperous economies, say they have been shocked by what they see as Beijing's influence in the territory.

"It seemed all right before when I saw Jiang Zemin, but now he is my president. When I saw Hong Kong people clapping after every phrase Jiang said, it seemed it was so easy for Hong Kong people to adapt," said a local professional, referring to a speech Jiang made at the handover ceremony.
"They seem to say, 'you want us to behave like you? That's all right. So you want to take our laws, that's all right too!'"
Results from a recent poll show more Hong Kong people, at 38.7 percent, preferred to call themselves "Hong Kongers", while 30.3 percent regarded themselves as Chinese.
But many Hong Kong people, particularly the elderly, have welcomed Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty.
"I'm very optimistic about Chinese rule. If you observe, China has never broken its word on any international agreement and it won't do it now," said security guard Wan Pak, 60.
"Hong Kong, with its financial position, is so important to China, so how could it let Hong Kong sink?"
Others were just happy to see the old colonial ruler depart. "I'm very happy, at least we're rid of the British," said Roy Lo, 50.
